one_liner: Seeded JavaScript/TypeScript PRNGs (xoroshiro128+, Mersenne Twister, LCG) with unbiased ranges; author's shuffle benchmark beats Math.random 1.4x.
what_it_does: Gives JS/TS code reproducible, seedable random numbers: four generators (congruential32, mersenne, xorshift128plus, xoroshiro128plus) plus unbiased uniformInt, uniformBigInt, uniformFloat32 and uniformFloat64 distributions, jump() for non-overlapping streams, and clone/getState/fromState for snapshotting. Since 8.0.0 (March 2026) generators are mutable objects whose next() returns a signed 32-bit integer and every function takes the generator as its first argument; the old pure style that returned [value, nextRng] is now opt-in through purify(), which clones the generator per call. It is not a drop-in for Math.random(): call sites must create and pass a generator, and next() yields an int32, not a double in [0, 1).
how_it_is_fast: Each 64-bit state word is kept as two 32-bit JavaScript numbers and advanced with |0, >>> and ^ so V8 stays in int32 arithmetic with no BigInt or allocation per draw (xoroshiro128plus.ts). congruential32 advances three LCG steps in parallel with Math.imul using precomputed a^2 and a^3 constants (8.4.1), and the 8.x releases also trimmed Mersenne Twister twisting, initialisation and allocations. uniformInt uses rejection sampling on one 32-bit draw followed by a modulo for ranges up to 2^32, with module-level scratch objects for wider ranges; it does not use Lemire's nearly divisionless method.
when_to_use: JS/TS code that needs seeded, replayable randomness: property-based tests, simulations, procedural generation, games with replays.
You need unbiased integer ranges (uniformInt) or 53-bit doubles (uniformFloat64) without writing your own rejection sampling, which Math.random-based Math.floor(r * n) code gets wrong.
You need independent parallel streams (jump() moves xoroshiro128plus 2^64 steps ahead) or need to serialize and restore generator state (getState / *FromState).
Functional or immutable codebases that want pure generator calls via purify() and accept a clone per call.
You already depend on fast-check: fast-check 4.10.2 lists pure-rand ^8.0.0 as its only dependency, so it adds no extra package.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: it is TypeScript compiled to JS and cannot be called from C++. Use a C++ generator from this category instead.
Anything security-sensitive (tokens, keys, shuffles with money at stake): none of the four generators is a CSPRNG; use crypto.getRandomValues.
Statistically demanding work that reads low bits: xoroshiro128plus next() returns the low 32 bits of the 64-bit s0+s1 sum, the bits the xoroshiro128+ literature reports as failing linearity tests.
Seeding many independent runs from random seeds: the xoroshiro128plus(seed) factory takes a 32-bit seed, so only 2^32 of its 2^128 states are reachable that way (use jump() for streams).
Bulk throughput: there is no typed-array fill; generateN returns a plain number[], and purify() allocates a clone on every call.

integration.form: module (npm package pure-rand, CommonJS and ESM builds, subpath exports only since 8.0.0, TypeScript types included)
integration.min_toolchain: No engines field; CI checks the bundle on Node 12.17.0 (test-legacy-bundle script). ES module subpath imports need a bundler or Node with exports-map support.
integration.platforms: any JavaScript runtime (Node, browsers, Deno/Bun not documented)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; since 8.0.0 generators mutate in place, so give each worker or logical stream its own instance (clone() or jump()).

gotchas: 8.0.0 is a breaking release: no main entry point (import from pure-rand/generator/... and pure-rand/distribution/...), rng moved to the first argument, mutation became the default, unsafeUniformIntDistribution became uniformInt, and fromState moved to xoroshiro128plusFromState and similar exports. The benchmark code (perf/compare.cjs at 556ec331) uses the 6.x names and will not run on 8.x.
next() returns a signed int32 in [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]; use >>> 0 for an unsigned value. uniformFloat64 consumes two next() calls per double.
The README's 'non-uniform' recipe ((rng.next() >>> 0) / 2^32 scaled by the range) is the variant that won the 1.4x benchmark and is biased; the README itself recommends against it.
Historic issues #1 (infinite loop when the range exceeded the generator) and #63 (non-uniform for gaps beyond 32 bits) are closed; no open bug or quality issues were listed on 2026-10-03.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when the code is JavaScript or TypeScript; the catalogued language-specific siblings fill the same role elsewhere (fastrand for Python, vpxyz/xorshift and pgregory.net/rand for Go, xrandom for Dart). For C++ use testingRNG's lehmer64 or aesctr, or SIMD generators such as simdrng or SHISHUA, plus FastShuffleExperiments for bounded integers, which use a nearly divisionless method where pure-rand uses a modulo.
verified_claims_summary: The author's COMPARISON.md times a Fisher-Yates shuffle of a 1,000,000-element array (tinybench, 1,000 iterations) on Node 16.19.1 on a 2-vCPU Xeon Platinum 8272CL GitHub Actions runner. With biased float scaling, pure-rand 6.0.0 xoroshiro128+ took 24.5 ms against 33.3 ms for Math.random (V8's xorshift128+), 28.1-33.5 ms for seedrandom and 109-143 ms for the faker and chance Mersenne Twisters. With unbiased ranges it took 53.5 ms against random-js MT19937 at 119.6 ms (2.2x). The figures are for pure-rand 6.0.0 (January 2023); 8.4.2 has not been re-measured in that document.
status_note: Active (8.4.2 released 2026-07-10, frequent performance commits), MIT, zero dependencies and the PRNG under fast-check, but JavaScript-only, so for this C++-first catalog it is a reference entry for JS projects.
